Melbourne SME recovery: where business presence remains weak

Group 10

23 October 2026

1. The question and the answer

Research question: Which precinct–industry groups in Melbourne show persistent SME establishment shortfalls, and how can their historical and recent recovery patterns inform priorities for further investigation and potential support?

The peer comparison supplement extends these results with same-industry comparisons outside each case’s precinct, historical context, and sensitivity to the screening cutoff and baseline year.

The Lord Mayor needs evidence to focus attention across a city with uneven business recovery. A rising city total can hide industries that continue to lose business locations. We examine changes across precincts and industries from 2002 to 2024, then compare the remaining gap from 2019 with recent change from 2022. This turns the broad recovery question into a specific review list.

We use Small and Medium establishments (1–199 jobs) throughout. An establishment is a business location. One company may operate several locations.

Three findings matter:

  • Recovery remains incomplete. The city had 13,054 SME establishments in 2024, 15.8% below 2019. The gain of 483 since 2022 offset 16.5% of the earlier loss.
  • The CBD and hospitality account for much of the recent increase. The CBD contributed 50.7% of the city net gain. Accommodation and Food Services contributed 44.3%. These describe different breakdowns of the same city total and should not be added together.
  • Five groups make the remaining weakness concrete. CBD professional services, finance, administrative support and construction have the largest 2019 shortfalls among groups that fell by at least 2% after 2022. Southbank hospitality shows that the hospitality recovery has not reached every precinct. Together, the five account for 876 fewer establishments than in 2019 and a further loss of 114 after 2022.

The recommendations follow these observed patterns. Forecast comparisons help explain why we have not used a model-generated ranking of future recovery.

2. What we did with the data

2.1 Coverage, variables and unit of analysis

The City of Melbourne’s Census of Land Use and Employment (CLUE) supplies two files covering 2002–2024. The aggregated file has 13,353 rows and 6 variables: census year, precinct, ANZSIC industry division, business size, establishment count and job count. A row is a year–precinct–industry–size combination containing a count of establishments. It does not represent an individual business.

Selecting Small and Medium categories retains 8,800 source rows, spanning 23 census years, 13 precincts and 19 industry divisions. We add the published Small and Medium counts within each year–precinct–industry group. For example, “CBD professional services in 2024” is one analytical group, containing 1,338 establishments. Large and non-employing businesses are outside the main population.

The address file contains 413,550 records and 12 fields, including census year, property identifiers, address, industry and coordinates. It supports all-size count checks. It has no business-size field, so we do not use it to identify individual SMEs or join business-level attributes onto the SME counts.

2.2 Preparation and data quality

We standardised names and types, checked the grouping keys for duplicates, and tested establishment counts for missing, negative or non-integer values. The aggregated file passed these checks. Precinct and industry totals were reconciled to the city total after selecting SMEs.

Job counts are missing in 4,252 aggregated rows (31.8%), all containing two or fewer establishments. This is consistent with confidentiality suppression. Their establishment counts are available, so we retain the rows and leave jobs missing. Jobs are not an outcome or predictor in this analysis.

The address file includes 68,299 Vacant Space records across all years. We retain the original records and separate this recorded category when checking operating-establishment totals. The aggregated SME file has no vacancy category. This step does not identify unrecorded closures or correct the survey cycle. The data audit records the checks and remaining differences between the two sources.

2.3 Why these years and comparisons?

Two-year-or-longer comparisons follow CLUE’s two-year property survey cycle. We use 2019 as the pre-pandemic reference, 2022 as the recent recovery starting point and 2024 as the latest supplied year. The city series gives longer-term context: 11,271 SMEs in 2002, 15,515 in 2017 and 15,506 in 2019. The near-flat 2017–2019 comparison helps distinguish the later shortfall from a long-running city-wide decline. These comparisons describe changes around the pandemic without estimating its causal effect.

An absent source combination stays unknown. The three-year descriptive screen has 206 complete groups out of 217 observed in at least one reference year. The other 11 cannot be classified by that screen. We report counts for small groups and withhold percentage comparisons where the relevant starting count is below 100. This is our reporting choice, not a CLUE rule. Small groups remain in city totals.

3. Where recovery is happening

3.1 The city is growing again, but remains below 2019

The count fell by 2,935 between 2019 and 2022, then rose by 483 by 2024. The remaining gap is 2,452 establishments. This is net change in establishment counts, not a count of closures or a causal estimate of COVID-19.

3.2 The CBD has the largest gap and the largest recent gain

All 13 precincts remained below their 2019 counts. 8 increased after 2022. The CBD accounts for 65.0% of the remaining city shortfall and added 245 recently. Large remaining losses and recent improvement can occur in the same precinct.

3.3 Hospitality gains coexist with continuing service-sector losses

Accommodation and Food Services added 214 establishments city-wide. Industry gains totalled 601; industry losses totalled 118, leaving a net gain of 483.

Within the CBD, hospitality increased by 180, while Professional, Scientific and Technical Services fell by 45. CBD professional services also had the largest precinct–industry shortfall from 2019, at 450. This makes the industry breakdown more informative than calling the whole CBD “recovered” or “declining”.

4. Five priority groups and why they matter

4.1 From 64 flagged groups to five specific cases

Our screen asks two questions: Was the 2024 count below 2019? Did it fall again between 2022 and 2024? 64 of the 206 comparable precinct–industry groups meet both conditions. Each group counts business locations in one industry within one precinct.

For closer review, we rank those groups by their absolute 2019–2024 shortfall and keep the four largest that also fell by at least 2% after 2022. All four are in the CBD. CBD health care ranks fourth by gap but lost only 3 establishments after 2022 (0.9%), so it goes to a watch list. The fifth case is the largest hospitality shortfall outside the CBD, Southbank: hospitality drives the city’s recovery, so a hospitality group that is still shrinking tests how far that recovery has spread. The rule favours gaps affecting more establishments; it does not estimate which policy would deliver the greatest benefit. The five account for 35.7% of the city’s remaining net shortfall. Other groups still matter: the full screen is exported, including 53 groups with a baseline below 100 in at least one comparison.

Precinct Industry 2019 2022 2024 2019-2024 change 2022-2024 change
Melbourne (CBD) Professional, Scientific and Technical Services 1,788 1,383 1,338 -25.2% -3.3%
Melbourne (CBD) Financial and Insurance Services 719 554 534 -25.7% -3.6%
Melbourne (CBD) Administrative and Support Services 381 243 219 -42.5% -9.9%
Melbourne (CBD) Construction 141 111 96 -31.9% -13.5%
Southbank Accommodation and Food Services 236 212 202 -14.4% -4.7%

4.2 What each case tells the City

Professional, Scientific and Technical Services: the largest remaining gap. The count fell from 1,788 to 1,338, leaving 450 fewer establishments than in 2019. It lost a further 45 after 2022, the largest recent decline among these five groups. Its scale makes it the clearest starting point for investigating weaker CBD business presence. Growth in CBD hospitality does not offset this industry’s loss of locations.

Financial and Insurance Services: a second substantial service-sector gap. Finance fell from 719 to 534 establishments, a 25.7% reduction. The additional loss of 20 after 2022 shows that the earlier shortfall was still widening. Together, finance and professional services place much of the remaining weakness in the CBD’s service economy.

Administrative and Support Services: the deepest proportional decline. This group fell from 381 to 219, down 42.5%. It also lost 24 establishments after 2022 (9.9%). Its smaller size than professional services should not obscure the much larger proportional loss. Both scale and recent direction support keeping it near the top of the City’s review list.

Construction: a smaller group with the sharpest recent percentage decline. Construction fell from 141 to 96 establishments. Its loss of 15 since 2022 represents 13.5%, the largest recent percentage decline among the five. The count measures construction business locations in the CBD; it does not measure construction output or the number of projects.

Southbank Accommodation and Food Services: the recovery has not reached the waterfront. The count fell from 236 to 202, including 10 after 2022 (4.7%), while CBD hospitality grew by 180 over the same period. Southbank’s weakness is therefore tied to the location, and a city-wide hospitality measure would mostly reach the CBD.

5. What prediction added

We tested whether historical counts could improve forecasts of each group’s next two-year change. The comparison used a no-change benchmark, multiple linear regression, a pruned regression tree and gradient boosting. Current count, its log transform, previous two-year change, precinct and industry were the predictors. Even-year observations provide consistent two-year steps aligned with the survey cycle.

Four expanding-window validation periods selected settings using mean absolute error (MAE). Outcomes from 2024 were excluded from model selection. Every selected model was then evaluated on the same 207 groups for 2022–2024.

Model MAE (establishments per group)
No change 5.13
Pruned tree 5.77
Gradient boosting 5.85
OLS 6.17

No change predicts that a group’s count stays at its starting level. It had the lowest average error among the tested methods. In the evaluation sample, 80.2% of groups changed by five establishments or fewer, which helps explain why the simple benchmark was competitive. That does not imply that the city stopped changing.

The baseline missed the matched sample’s net increase of 481 establishments, and its error was much larger for large groups. We therefore make no model-based 2026 forecast. Observed shortfalls and recent changes support the recommendations. Full model settings, sample coverage and error diagnostics are in Appendix A.

6. Recommendations and conclusion

Focus the first review on CBD professional services, finance and administrative support. Together they have 797 fewer establishments than in 2019 and lost a further 89 after 2022. They combine the largest historical gaps with continuing losses. This gives the City a specific set of industries to consider when setting SME support priorities.

Treat construction and Southbank hospitality separately. CBD construction has the sharpest recent percentage decline of the five. Southbank hospitality is a local weakness in an industry that is growing in the CBD. CBD health care stays on a watch list because its count has barely moved since 2022.

Use the precinct–industry breakdown when discussing recovery. The CBD added 245 SMEs overall, including 180 in hospitality, while the four CBD cases lost 104. City growth and continuing local weakness coexist. The same breakdown should guide consideration of the remaining screened groups outside these five cases.

The study identifies where business presence has weakened and how the pattern differs across groups. Choosing a particular grant, incentive or funding amount requires evidence on business needs and intervention costs that CLUE does not provide. Policy implementation schedules and programme evaluation are outside this report’s scope.

Appendix A. Predictive methods and diagnostics

A.1 Target, predictors and models

For each precinct–industry group:

Target change = establishments at t+2 − establishments at t.

For example, a count of 100 rising to 108 gives a target of +8. No change predicts a target of zero, equivalent to predicting that 100 establishments remain. Its absolute error in this example is 8.

The fitted models use five predictors available at the starting date: the current count, log(1 + current count), the previous two-year change, precinct and industry. The log term allows OLS to describe a curved size relationship without forcing the effect of size to be purely proportional.

  • No change: a simple benchmark with no fitted coefficients.
  • Multiple linear regression (OLS): a transparent additive relationship between the predictors and the next change.
  • Pruned regression tree: thresholds and interactions, with pruning chosen from historical validation rather than random cross-validation.
  • Gradient boosting: a small ensemble of shallow regression trees, tested to see whether added flexibility improves prediction.

Every method is assessed on identical cells. Predicted changes are bounded below by minus the starting count, so a forecast cannot imply a negative number of establishments. Predictions are not rounded before scoring.

A.2 Keep later outcomes out of model selection

We grow the training window forward through time. For a prediction made at year t, training can use only changes whose outcome year is at or before t. The train/test separation applies to time, not a random selection of rows.

Training origins Last observed training outcome Validation period Training rows
2004-2012 2014 2014-2016 1042
2004-2014 2016 2016-2018 1247
2004-2016 2018 2018-2020 1450
2004-2018 2020 2020-2022 1657

The tree grid tests pruning parameters 0.001, 0.01 and 0.05, with minimum leaf sizes of 5 or 10. Boosting tests depths 1 or 2 and 100 or 300 trees, with a learning rate of 0.03. No random subsampling is used.

We average the four validation MAEs, giving each historical period equal weight. That selects a configuration within each model family and an overall model before the 2022–2024 evaluation. The selected model is No change. These are reconstructed historical tests using the supplied data vintage, not a prospective test on newly observed outcomes.

A.3 Results on the 2022–2024 evaluation

Model Cells MAE RMSE Mean error Selected before test
No change 207 5.13 15.45 -2.32 TRUE
Pruned tree 207 5.77 20.91 -3.26 FALSE
Gradient boosting 207 5.85 22.22 -4.04 FALSE
OLS 207 6.17 20.22 -4.34 FALSE

MAE is the average absolute error, in establishments per group. RMSE gives large errors more weight. Mean error is predicted minus actual change: negative values indicate underprediction.

The evaluation includes 207 of 210 published starting groups and 100.0% of their establishments. The matched sample gained 481 establishments, compared with 483 for the city. Coverage tables account for the difference; it is not silently treated as zero.

The baseline wins on test MAE and RMSE in this rebuild. Historical validation RMSE and MAE do not always rank models in the same order; the model-selection rule was MAE throughout. The complete validation leaderboard is exported.

A.4 Why no change performs well, and where it is weak

80.2% of evaluation groups changed by five establishments or fewer. 56.0% started with fewer than 20 establishments. Predicting zero can keep errors small across many such groups without estimating extra relationships.

That is a pattern in the evaluation sample, not proof that every group is stable. Only 21.3% had exactly zero change. Large changes still matter.

The ten largest errors account for 45.9% of total absolute error. The no-change prediction misses the matched sample’s net gain of 481. We therefore use it as a benchmark, while using observed local gaps and recent changes to support investigation priorities. A zero-change forecast cannot rank which groups will recover fastest.

A.5 What changes when non-employing establishments are included?

Scope Model Matched cells MAE RMSE Observed net change

Small + Medium No change 207 5.13 15.45 481
Small + Medium OLS 207 6.17 20.22 481
Small + Medium Pruned tree 207 5.77 20.91 481
Small + Medium + Non employing Gradient boosting 207 5.84 21.14 458
Small + Medium + Non employing No change 207 5.12 14.94 458

This check holds each model family’s main-analysis configuration fixed and compares identical group keys. It changes the population, so its counts and error sizes should not replace the main results. The separate data audit compares descriptive results under both definitions.

Appendix B. Supplementary industry-mix comparison

We compare each precinct with the same industries elsewhere in the city. For each matched industry, we multiply the local starting count by the rest-of-city industry’s observed growth factor. We then sum the comparison counts over the same cells as the observed counts.

A negative value means local growth was below that descriptive comparison. It suggests a question for local investigation without estimating the effect of a precinct, COVID-19 or a policy. It is supplementary to the five-case selection and does not determine that ranking.

The chart requires at least 95% count coverage in both years and a starting count of 100. These are our reporting thresholds. The exported tables also repeat the comparison after requiring 100 establishments in each rest-of-city reference industry, to check sensitivity to small reference groups.

Appendix C. Audit trail and reproduction

The report is generated from R Markdown, which runs the calculations and inserts the resulting tables and figures. The supplied CSV files remain unchanged. Source checksums, package versions and test results are saved with the analysis outputs.

Run from the repository root:

Rscript scripts/install_dependencies.R
Rscript scripts/run_final_analysis.R

The first command installs missing packages once. The second runs both test suites and rebuilds the data audit, final analysis, charts and exported results. No packages or source datasets are downloaded during analysis.

The code checks duplicate keys, invalid counts, source-file hashes, missing cells, reconciliation, identical evaluation samples, exact two-year alignment, and temporal leakage. A test changes the held-out outcomes and confirms that all four models’ predictions remain unchanged.

Key files:

  • scripts/descriptive_followup.R: counts, contributions, industry-mix comparison and observed review lists.
  • scripts/predictive_models.R: panel construction, validation, fitting and errors.
  • tests/test_final_analysis.R: independent calculations and failure-case tests.
  • outputs/tables/final/: every score, prediction, exclusion, setting and figure.

The report uses the supplied 2002–2024 snapshot. It does not estimate individual business survival, policy effects, employment growth or the causal effect of COVID-19. There are only four validation periods and one final evaluation period. The error rankings do not establish statistical significance.

Sources and assistance

City of Melbourne: aggregated CLUE dataset and address-level dataset. The supplied files, rather than live downloads, are used here.

Hyndman and Athanasopoulos, Forecasting: Principles and Practice, Chapter 5: naive benchmarks, forecast errors and rolling-origin evaluation. rpart documentation and gbm documentation describe the fitted tree methods.

Claude (Anthropic) reviewed and extended the R code and edited the data sections. Codex (OpenAI) reviewed earlier versions of the R scripts. See docs/AI_ASSISTANCE.md. The group is responsible for the submission.
